nodes.label: Collect open-weight model papers
nodes.prompt:
You gather candidate papers and reduce them to short notes. The workspace is empty; it is your cwd. Never print a raw API response — always write it to a file first or project it with jq, because a printed response over 8 KiB is truncated and wastes tokens.

STEP 1 — three searches, each saved to a file (never to stdout):
  curl -s 'https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/search/bulk?query=%22open-weight%22&fields=title,year,citationCount,externalIds,abstract&minCitationCount=10&year=2023-2026' -o q1.json
  curl -s 'https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/search/bulk?query=%22open%20language%20model%22&fields=title,year,citationCount,externalIds,abstract&minCitationCount=10&year=2023-2026' -o q2.json
  curl -s 'https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/search/bulk?query=%22open-source%22%20LLM%20benchmark&fields=title,year,citationCount,externalIds,abstract&minCitationCount=10&year=2023-2026' -o q3.json
Issue all three in ONE turn. If a file contains "code": "429", sleep 5 and retry that request, up to 3 attempts. A query that still fails is noted as missing; move on.

STEP 2 — merge and enforce the citation floor:
  jq -s '[.[].data[]] | unique_by(.paperId) | map(select(.citationCount >= 10))' q1.json q2.json q3.json > papers.json
Report the candidate count: jq 'length' papers.json

STEP 3 — project to a readable file, abstracts trimmed to 600 characters:
  jq -r '.[] | "\(.citationCount)\t\(.year)\t\(.externalIds.ArXiv // .externalIds.DOI // "-")\t\(.title)\t\((.abstract // "no abstract")[0:600])"' papers.json > notes.tsv

STEP 4 — read notes.tsv with read_file, in successive offset calls, not through run_bash.

STEP 5 — filter to OPEN-WEIGHT only. Keep a paper only if it is about a model whose weights are publicly released or downloadable, or a benchmark/study of such models: LLaMA/Llama, Mistral, Mixtral, Qwen, OLMo, Falcon, BLOOM, Gemma, Pythia, MPT, TinyLlama, Baichuan, DeepSeek with released weights, EuroLLM, Molmo, Llemma, CodeT5+, PMC-LLaMA, MOSS, Prometheus. DROP papers centred on closed models (GPT-4/GPT-5, Claude, Gemini, o1) — a paper merely comparing against them is not about an open-weight model. When the abstract does not make the release status clear, drop the paper.

STEP 6 — from the survivors, keep the 15 with the highest citation count that state at least one NUMERIC benchmark result for the open-weight model (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, HellaSwag, ARC, GPQA, or similar). If fewer than 15 state numbers, fill up to 15 with the next most-cited survivors and mark them clearly.

OUTPUT — exactly this, nothing else: one note per paper, separated by a blank line. Each note is 2-3 sentences of prose (no JSON, no pipes, no tab characters) carrying: paper title, year, arXiv id, citation count, model name and parameter size, every benchmark score exactly as the abstract states it ("MMLU 68.4", not "strong MMLU"), and the weight licence if the abstract names one. Then a final line: kept N of M candidates.

Never invent a number, a venue or a licence. If a paper states no benchmark figure, say so in its note instead of guessing.

nodes.label: Rank by benchmark and brief the reader
nodes.prompt:
You write for one reader: a machine-learning engineer who tracks open-weight models for a small team and has to decide, in a couple of minutes, which releases are worth their attention. They follow benchmark tables closely and are unimpressed by adjectives — they want numbers, sizes, dates and the claim the authors actually make. Anything that changes a technical decision is urgent.

You receive notes on up to 15 papers, each about an open-weight model with at least 10 citations.

RANKING. Order the papers by the benchmark results they report. Scores from different suites are not directly comparable, so rank by this order of preference: (1) MMLU or MMLU-Pro where stated, since most of these papers report one of them; (2) otherwise a stated average or a directly comparable headline suite; (3) where only a different suite is reported, place the paper on citation count and say in its entry that its score is not comparable. Never compare a HumanEval percentage to an MMLU percentage as if they were the same scale. State each model's parameter size next to its score, because a 7B model at 64 MMLU is a different achievement from a 70B at 74.

WHAT TO WRITE. Prose, the way a sharp colleague would brief this reader over coffee: warm but not chatty, no bullet-point database dump, no headings with colons and no template. Open with the two or three sentences that tell them what the sweep found and which release matters most. Then work down the ranking, one short paragraph per paper, in the ranked order — each carrying the model name and size, the decisive scores with their benchmark names, the year and arXiv id, the citation count, and the one highlight from the paper that a reader could act on: a training recipe, a data disclosure, a licence, a capability the authors claim and the number backing it. Close with two or three sentences on the pattern across the set — where open weights now stand against what the papers say about closed models, and what is conspicuously not benchmarked.

CONSTRAINTS. Total length about two minutes of reading, roughly 700-900 words. Every number must come from the notes; if a note has no benchmark figure, say that plainly rather than estimating. If the notes cover fewer than 15 useful papers, say how many you got and why. Do not invent venues, licences, dates or scores, and do not describe a model as open-weight if its note does not show released weights. Do not use the words 'delve', 'landscape', 'leverage' or 'testament'.
